Benchmarking against other sparse PCA packages

Source: vignettes/articles/benchmarking.Rmd
benchmarking.Rmd

This vignette gives the benchmarking protocol and results behind the summary in the package description. It compares msPCA against seven competing implementations on four real datasets, and records how each competitor was configured. That configuration matters more than usual here, because the packages parameterise sparsity in mutually incompatible ways.

Chunks are not evaluated at build time. Reproducing the comparison requires eight additional R packages, callr, and a Python installation, and the memory measurements require macOS or Linux. The scripts are in the package repository under replication/benchmarking/.

Getting the data

All four datasets are obtainable from R without manual downloads or accounts, so the comparison is reproducible end to end:

## mtcars -- base R
X_mtcars     <- as.matrix(datasets::mtcars)
Sigma_mtcars <- cor(X_mtcars)

## Pitprops -- the 13 x 13 correlation matrix of Jeffers (1967), Table 1.
## It is transcribed literally at the top of
## replication/benchmarking/notebook_pitprops.R; source that file to obtain `pitprops`.
Sigma_pitprops <- pitprops
## Methods that require a data matrix instead use pseudo-data drawn from this
## correlation structure (see "How each method was configured" below).
set.seed(42)
X_pitprops <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = 500, mu = rep(0, ncol(pitprops)),
                            Sigma = pitprops)

## Breast cancer -- one-off download via PMA, then keep the 500 highest-
## variance genes, following the preprocessing of Witten et al. (2009).
X            <- t(PMA::download_breast_data(
  url = "https://tibshirani.su.domains/PMA/breastdata.rda")$rna)
X_breast     <- X[, order(apply(X, 2, var), decreasing = TRUE)[1:500]]
Sigma_breast <- cor(X_breast)          # n = 89, p = 500

## Riboflavin -- ships with the hdi package
data("riboflavin", package = "hdi")
X_ribo <- as.matrix(riboflavin$x)      # n = 71, p = 4088

Only the breast cancer data touches the network, and PMA::download_breast_data() handles it in a single call. Riboflavin ships inside hdi, mtcars is in base R, and the Pitprops correlation matrix is transcribed in the benchmarking script, so no manual downloads or accounts are needed anywhere.

Methods compared

We compare msPCA::mspca() against seven competing functions. Each entry below names the exact function called, not merely the package, since several packages expose more than one sparse PCA routine and nsprcomp in particular provides two with quite different behaviour.

Function Reference Language Approach
elasticnet::spca() Zou et al. (2006) R elastic-net regularization, LARS-like
PMA::SPC() Witten et al. (2009) R penalized matrix decomposition
sparsepca::spca() Erichson et al. (2020) R variable projection with ℓ1\ell_1 penalty
mixOmics::spca() Rohart et al. (2017) R regularized SVD (Shen and Huang 2008)
nsprcomp::nsprcomp() Sigg (2019) R expectation-maximization (Sigg and Buhmann 2008) + deflation
nsprcomp::nscumcomp() Sigg (2019) R cumulative variant, all components jointly
amanpg::spca.amanpg() Chen et al. (2020) R alternating manifold proximal gradient
sklearn.decomposition.SparsePCA() Pedregosa et al. (2011) Python dictionary learning

scikit-learn is called from R via the reticulate package (Ushey et al. 2025). Together these cover the main methodological approaches to sparse PCA: elastic-net regularization, penalized matrix decomposition, variable-projection optimization, regularized SVD, deflation, Riemannian proximal gradient, and dictionary learning.

How each function obtains multiple components, and what its tuning parameter controls

The comparison turns on two things that are easy to conflate: how a method gets from one sparse component to rr of them, and what the parameter the user actually turns is doing. The second column below states the mechanism; the last two classify the parameter we tune as controlling sparsity, optimization convergence, an orthogonality penalty, or a feasibility tolerance.

Function Multiple-component mechanism Parameter tuned What it controls
msPCA::mspca() Iterative deflation heuristic; all rr components are refined together, with the non-redundancy constraint enforced across every pair and its penalty tightened over the iterations ks Sparsity — exact cardinality, one budget per component
elasticnet::spca() All rr jointly: alternates an orthonormal Procrustes update of an auxiliary factor with per-component elastic-net regressions. Orthonormality is imposed on the auxiliary factor, not on the returned sparse loadings para (with sparse = "varnum") Sparsity — exact cardinality per component
PMA::SPC() Sequential rank-1 penalized matrix decompositions with deflation. orth = TRUE selects the variant of Section 3.2 of Witten et al. (2009), which requires the left factors 𝒖k\boldsymbol{u}_k to be mutually orthogonal — not the sparse loadings 𝒗k\boldsymbol{v}_k that the function returns and that we score sumabsv Sparsity — an ℓ1\ell_1 bound on each loading vector, not a cardinality
sparsepca::spca() All rr jointly, by variable projection on the SPCA objective alpha Sparsity — magnitude of the ℓ1\ell_1 penalty, with no per-component control
mixOmics::spca() Sequential regularized rank-1 SVDs with deflation keepX Sparsity — exact number of variables retained per component
nsprcomp::nsprcomp() Sequential cardinality-constrained components via an EM-style iteration, combined with the deflation of Mackey (2008) k Sparsity — exact cardinality per component
nsprcomp::nscumcomp() All rr jointly, under one cumulative budget k, gamma k: sparsity, as a total budget ∑tkt\sum_t k_t; gamma: orthogonality penalty, which we tune (see below) rather than leaving at its default of 0
amanpg::spca.amanpg() All rr jointly: alternates a proximal-gradient step on the sparse loadings with a manifold update of an orthonormal factor on the Stiefel manifold lambda1 Sparsity — a vector of per-component ℓ1\ell_1 penalties
sklearn...SparsePCA() All n_components jointly, by dictionary learning alpha Sparsity — magnitude of the ℓ1\ell_1 penalty on the loadings

Two things stand out from that table.

Every competing function is tuned through sparsity alone. Four of them (elasticnet::spca(), mixOmics::spca(), nsprcomp::nsprcomp() and msPCA::mspca()) accept an exact cardinality per component and hit it. The others expose a penalty magnitude (sparsepca::spca(), amanpg::spca.amanpg(), sklearn...SparsePCA()), an ℓ1\ell_1 bound (PMA::SPC()), or a single cumulative budget they distribute as they see fit (nsprcomp::nscumcomp()). Their realised sparsity patterns consequently miss the target, often by a wide margin and unevenly across components: (68,1,2) and (22,3,1) on breast cancer, against a request of (20,20,20).

Only nsprcomp::nscumcomp() offers any control over non-redundancy, through the soft penalty gamma, whose default of 0 applies no penalty at all. We tune gamma by a different rule from the sparsity parameters: among values bringing the orthogonality violation within 1e-4, keep the one with the highest FVE. The question that answers is “at equal feasibility, how much variance does each method explain?”

gamma does work, on all three datasets where nscumcomp appears, but the penalties required are extreme (10^6 on mtcars, 10^7 on Pitprops), the runtime cost reaches fortyfold, and the resulting solutions still miss the requested per-component cardinality.

PMA::SPC()’s orth switch is not a second exception. It orthogonalises the left factors 𝒖k\boldsymbol{u}_k; the sparse loadings 𝒗k\boldsymbol{v}_k it returns carry no orthogonality guarantee either way. No competing function exposes a feasibility tolerance: a value the user sets to say how orthogonal the components must be, which the method then attains. That is what msPCA::mspca()’s feasibilityTolerance (default 1e-4) is, and nscumcomp reaches the same target only through a search over gamma conducted outside the package.

Convergence controls (maxIter and stallingTolerance in msPCA::mspca(), em_tol/em_maxiter/nrestart in nsprcomp, tol/maxiter in amanpg, tol/max_iter in scikit-learn) govern optimization convergence rather than sparsity or feasibility. All are left at package defaults, except maxIter = 100 for msPCA::mspca() on riboflavin.

Environment

Experiments were conducted on a MacBook Air with an Apple M2 chip and 24 GB of RAM, with R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24), msPCA v0.5.1, elasticnet v1.3, PMA v1.2.4, sparsepca v0.1.2, mixOmics v6.36.0, nsprcomp v0.5.1.2, amanpg v0.3.4, reticulate v1.46.0, callr v3.8.0, and scikit-learn v1.6.1 (Python 3.11). Full session information is recorded in replication/sessionInfo.txt.

Configuration

The table above gives each function’s mechanism and tuning parameter. What remains to be fixed is which input each one receives, since some accept a covariance or correlation matrix, some require the data matrix, and some take either.

  • msPCA::mspca() — run with both type = "Sigma" and type = "X" on all four datasets. On riboflavin (n≪pn \ll p) the p×pp \times p covariance matrix is rank-deficient, making type = "X" the natural choice; we report both modes to quantify the runtime and memory gain.
  • elasticnet::spca() — takes a list of cardinality budgets (one per PC) via sparse = "varnum", and applies interchangeably to 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} (type = "Gram") or 𝑿\boldsymbol{X} (type = "predictor"). We report both input modes on mtcars, Pitprops and breast cancer.
  • PMA::SPC() — applied to the data matrix on all three datasets, as documented (x is “a data matrix of dimension n×pn \times p”, and SPC() centres its columns itself). On Pitprops that means the pseudo-data, since no real data matrix exists. sumabsv bounds the ℓ1\ell_1 norm of each loading vector (subject to unit ℓ2\ell_2 norm) and must lie between 1 and p\sqrt{p}; we tune it per dataset to bring per-component sparsity as close to the target as the parameterization allows. We set orth = TRUE, which selects the multiple-component variant of Section 3.2 of Witten et al. (2009); note that this orthogonalises the left factors 𝒖k\boldsymbol{u}_k rather than the sparse loadings 𝒗k\boldsymbol{v}_k we extract, so the orthogonality violations reported for PMA::SPC() below are not a failure to deliver something the function promised.
  • sparsepca::spca() — applied to 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}. It exposes only the magnitude of the ℓ1\ell_1 penalty alpha, which we tune per dataset to achieve a total sparsity ∑tkt\sum_t k_t close to the target. This method tends to return PCs with very unequal sparsity levels, the first typically denser than the rest.
  • mixOmics::spca() — takes the data matrix and the list of per-component budgets keepX, so it hits the cardinality target exactly.
  • nsprcomp::nsprcomp() and nsprcomp::nscumcomp() — two functions from the same package, both based on the EM algorithm of Sigg and Buhmann (2008), which behave differently enough that we report them separately. nsprcomp() computes the leading sparse PC then applies the deflation procedure of Mackey (2008) for subsequent PCs; it takes the data matrix and a vector of per-component cardinalities. nscumcomp() solves for all rr PCs simultaneously under a single cumulative budget ∑tkt\sum_t k_t, which it distributes as it sees fit, plus the penalty gamma on divergence from orthonormality.
  • amanpg::spca.amanpg() — accepts either input and is told which via type: type = 0 declares z to be a data matrix, any non-zero value declares it a covariance matrix. We use type = 1 with the correlation matrix on mtcars and Pitprops, where the correlation matrix is the natural object, and type = 0 with the data matrix on breast cancer. It computes all rr components jointly, alternating a proximal-gradient step on the sparse loadings with a manifold update of an orthonormal factor on the Stiefel manifold; lambda1 is a vector of per-component ℓ1\ell_1 penalties, which we tune per dataset, and we set lambda2 = Inf.
  • sklearn.decomposition.SparsePCA() — called via reticulate. The class computes n_components components simultaneously using dictionary learning with an ℓ1\ell_1 penalty alpha on the loadings, applied to the data matrix. We tune alpha per dataset and fix random_state to the repetition’s seed.

For Pitprops only the correlation matrix is available, so we generate pseudo-data via MASS::mvrnorm() with the Pitprops matrix as the population covariance (n=500n = 500) for the methods that require 𝑿\boldsymbol{X} — mixOmics::spca(), nsprcomp::nsprcomp(), nsprcomp::nscumcomp(), PMA::SPC() and sklearn...SparsePCA(). FVE and the orthogonality violation are always evaluated against the published Pitprops correlation matrix, never against the covariance of the pseudo-data.

Every tuning parameter is selected by the scripts rather than fixed by hand: each is swept over a grid and the value whose realised sparsity comes closest to the target is kept, with ties broken on FVE and candidates that leave a component empty discarded. The selected values appear beneath each table. Tuning is excluded from all reported runtimes and memory figures.

How runtime and memory are measured

Every repetition of every method runs in its own fresh R process, driven by replication/benchmarking/bench_utils.R. Isolation is necessary because peak memory is read as a process-level high-water mark: several methods in one session, or even several repetitions of one method, contaminate each other.

Memory is peak resident set size, obtained from getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss. R-level metrics such as gc() or bench::mark(mem_alloc) are deliberately not used: msPCA does its work in RcppEigen buffers and scikit-learn in the embedded CPython heap, neither of which R’s garbage collector observes, so an R-level metric would under-report exactly those two methods while fully charging the pure-R competitors. The Memory column below reports the working set, defined as the size of the matrix handed to the method plus the additional peak RSS the method allocates on top of it. The R interpreter and package-loading floor are excluded, so the column is comparable across methods but is not the absolute footprint of the session. It does include whatever a package allocates on its first call — lazy loading of namespaces, compiled code, S4 method tables — which is on the order of 4 MB.

No warm-up call precedes the measurement, so the ~4 MB of first-call loading is charged to every method. That is deliberate. Any allocation beforehand leaves R’s garbage collector with higher heap growth targets, so the measured run collects less often and peaks higher, inflating the methods that allocate on R’s heap while leaving msPCA and scikit-learn untouched. Carrying the loading cost is the smaller distortion.

Each method is repeated five times with a different seed. Runtime, memory, FVE and the orthogonality violation are reported as medians, with a bracketed range wherever the spread exceeds 15%.

Those ranges matter, because neither runtime nor peak RSS is reproducible to the precision a bare median implies. Wall-clock time varies with machine load and with seed-dependent iteration counts. Peak RSS varies with garbage-collector timing: repeated runs of the Pitprops script, at identical seeds and with bit-identical FVE and orthogonality, put nscumcomp’s working set anywhere between 72 and 211 MB. For the pure-R methods even the median of five moves by a factor of two between sittings, so read their memory figures as order-of-magnitude. msPCA is the exception: it allocates in Eigen rather than on R’s heap, and its figures reproduce to within a few percent.

# Representative call pattern; see replication/benchmarking/ for the full scripts.
set.seed(42)
res <- mspca(Sigma, r = 3, ks = rep(4, 3), verbose = FALSE)

fraction_variance_explained(Sigma, res$x_best)
feasibility_violation_off(Sigma, res$x_best, 0)
res$runtime

Thirty-one of the forty sparsepca candidates and five of the sklearn candidates were rejected for leaving a component empty.

nscumcomp performs well here once gamma is tuned. At 0.824 it is the second-best sparse method by FVE, and at 1.1e-05 one of the few inside the feasibility tolerance, though it returns (5,5,2) rather than the requested (4,4,4). At its default gamma = 0 the same call gives a violation of 0.242.

Only nscumcomp varies across seeds, over 0.798–0.825 in FVE, with a worst-case violation of 3.3e-05 that remains inside tolerance. Every other method, msPCA included, returns the same solution at every seed.

At p=11p = 11 the numerical working set of every method is a few kilobytes, so the memory column measures fixed overheads rather than algorithmic cost. Most methods sit at or below 1.6 MB. elasticnet, sparsepca and nscumcomp do not: each carries a floor of 17–30 MB already present at this size, of which only about 4 MB is first-call loading.

Pitprops

The Pitprops dataset (Jeffers 1967) (p=13p = 13 physical measurements on n=180n = 180 timber specimens) is a classic sparse PCA benchmark (e.g. Zou et al. 2006). We extract r=6r = 6 sparse PCs targeting k=4k = 4 nonzero loadings per component, as in Zou et al. (2006).

elasticnet::spca (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) (4,4,4,4,4,4) 0.790 0.322 0.158 78 [70, 83]

sparsepca::spca (7,3,4,2,4,4) 0.756 0.353 0.039 28

nsprcomp::nsprcomp (4,4,4,4,4,4) 0.816 0.563 0.025 [0.023, 0.028] 33 [32, 39]

Tuning selected automatically: PMA::SPC sumabsv = 1.55; sparsepca::spca alpha = 0.005; amanpg::spca.amanpg lambda1 = c(4.80, 4.40, 1.95, 5.50, 0.20, 0.05); sklearn...SparsePCA alpha = 2.6; nsprcomp::nscumcomp gamma = 1e7. The spread in amanpg’s penalty vector, from 5.50 down to 0.05, tracks the decay of the spectrum; a single shared value cannot reproduce it.

nscumcomp needs γ=107\gamma = 10^7, seven orders of magnitude above its default, to bring its orthogonality violation to 5.1e-05 from the 1.87 it returns at γ=0\gamma = 0. That costs 0.026 of FVE and a fortyfold slowdown, and the resulting sparsity is (5,6,5,2,4,2) rather than the requested (4,4,4,4,4,4).

Across seeds, msPCA (𝚺)(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) ranges over 0.786–0.822 in FVE and msPCA (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) over 0.784–0.801, both holding the orthogonality violation below 1e-04 at every seed. nsprcomp ranges over 0.813–0.833 with a worst-case violation of 1.105, and nscumcomp over 0.814–0.830 with a worst case of 1.03e-04. This is the one dataset where msPCA is visibly stochastic, an artefact of the random restarts in the truncated power method; feasibility is what does not vary.

This is also the dataset where the feasibility differences are starkest. With p=13p = 13 and a total budget of 24 nonzeros, trivially orthogonal disjoint-support solutions do not exist, so methods that rely on deflation have nothing to fall back on: at the requested cardinality, elasticnet, mixOmics and nsprcomp return violations of 0.215–0.563 against 9.7e-05 for msPCA. Only nscumcomp, with gamma driven to 10710^7, also reaches the tolerance — and it does so at a cardinality that misses the budget.

Pitprops is the one case where type = "X" is the wrong choice: with n=500n = 500 pseudo-observations and p=13p = 13, the data matrix is larger than the correlation matrix, and the O(np)O(np) matrix-free product is more expensive than the O(p2)O(p^2) dense one. Runtime is roughly six times worse than the type = "Sigma" path, though at this scale the memory difference is below what the measurement can resolve. The interface is a win when n≪pn \ll p, not universally.

Tuning selected automatically: PMA::SPC sumabsv = 3.3; sparsepca::spca alpha = 0.0035; amanpg::spca.amanpg lambda1 = c(4.5, 1.8, 3.3); sklearn...SparsePCA alpha = 15; nsprcomp::nscumcomp gamma = 316, with a total budget of k=60k = 60 that it distributes unevenly. gamma matters far less here than on the small datasets, because at p=500p = 500 with 60 nonzeros in total the supports are nearly disjoint anyway.

This is the dataset where the penalty-parameterized methods break down most clearly. No value on the grid lets amanpg::spca.amanpg() approach (20,20,20): the best available is (68,1,2), a deviation of 85, and the two trailing components are all but empty. sklearn...SparsePCA() reaches (22,3,1), and sparsepca::spca() (43,14,22). Only the four functions that accept an exact cardinality — msPCA, elasticnet, mixOmics and nsprcomp::nsprcomp — return the budget that was asked for.

Across seeds, msPCA ranges over 0.088–0.095 in FVE in both input modes, with the orthogonality violation at or below 9.8e-05 at every seed. nsprcomp ranges over 0.070–0.084, nscumcomp over 0.080–0.085, and sklearn...SparsePCA over 0.020–0.032.

With p=500p = 500 and 60 nonzeros in total, disjoint supports are easy to find, so most methods are trivially orthogonal here and the feasibility column carries little information.

This is the smallest dataset at which the memory column measures the algorithms rather than fixed overheads. msPCA is the lightest of the sparse methods that meet the budget: 7.1 MB on the correlation matrix and 3.1 MB on the data matrix, against 209 MB for elasticnet in Gram mode, 79 MB on the data matrix, 92 MB for sparsepca, and 48–57 MB for nsprcomp and nscumcomp. mixOmics at 7.0 MB is comparable, and sklearn lighter still at 0.6 MB, though it allocates outside R entirely and returns (22,3,1) rather than the requested budget. The type = "X" saving is modest here because 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} is only about 2 MB at p=500p = 500. Riboflavin is where it becomes decisive.

Riboflavin

The riboflavin (vitamin B2) production dataset (Bühlmann et al. 2014) comprises log-transformed expression levels of p=4,088p = 4{,}088 genes in n=71n = 71 samples of Bacillus subtilis. This is a challenging p≫np \gg n benchmark: the empirical correlation matrix is rank-deficient (rank ≤70\leq 70). We set r=2r = 2 and target k=20k = 20 nonzero loadings per component. To avoid time-consuming parameter tuning, we consider only methods that accept exact cardinality budgets.

Method (k1,k2)(k_1, k_2) FVE Orth. violation Runtime (s) Memory (MB)
msPCA::mspca (𝚺)(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) (20,20) 0.008 < 1e-15 59.504 [50.630, 99.328] 641
msPCA::mspca (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) (20,20) 0.008 < 1e-15 1.842 [0.891, 2.563] 45
elasticnet::spca (𝑿)(\boldsymbol{X}) (20,20) 0.004 < 1e-15 6.894 309 [307, 426]
mixOmics::spca (20,20) 0.006 < 1e-15 0.334 24 [20, 24]
nsprcomp::nsprcomp (20,20) 0.009 < 1e-15 0.353 [0.266, 0.371] 59
PCA (dense) (4088,4088) 0.478 < 1e-15 0.046 39

msPCA is run with maxIter = 100 here; all methods other than msPCA (𝚺)(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) use the data matrix directly. Only msPCA varies at all across seeds, and only in the third decimal of FVE (0.008–0.009 in both input modes).

This dataset isolates the benefit of the type = "X" interface. Passing the raw data matrix replaces the O(p2)O(p^2) product 𝚺𝜷\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\beta} with the O(np)O(np) two-pass product 𝑿⊤(𝑿𝜷)/(n−1)\boldsymbol{X}^\top(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})/(n-1) and never forms the covariance matrix. The measured working set falls from 641 MB to 45 MB, a factor of about 14, at identical FVE and feasibility. The p×pp \times p correlation matrix accounts for 128 MB of that, the remainder being the Eigen copy of it and the dense intermediates the O(p2)O(p^2) path requires. Median runtime falls from 59.5 seconds to 1.8, a factor of about 30, though both rows vary by a factor of two or more across seeds and one significant figure is all the ratio will support.

The memory figures over those same repetitions span 639–642 MB, a spread of well under one percent. The contrast holds throughout: msPCA allocates in Eigen, where the footprint follows from the algorithm, so its memory requirement can be predicted from nn, pp and rr. The pure-R methods allocate on R’s heap, where the peak depends on garbage-collector timing, and elasticnet’s median on this dataset has landed anywhere between 309 and 570 MB on repeated runs of the identical script.

Together with the Pitprops result the rule is simply the relative size of the two inputs: use type = "X" when n≪pn \ll p, and type = "Sigma" when p≲np \lesssim n.

Discussion

Sparsity control. PMA::SPC(), sparsepca::spca(), nsprcomp::nscumcomp(), amanpg::spca.amanpg() and sklearn.decomposition.SparsePCA() give no direct control over the sparsity of each loading vector. PMA::SPC() and sklearn expose only a global ℓ1\ell_1 bound; sparsepca::spca(), nscumcomp() and amanpg tend to return unbalanced components, with one PC carrying most of the budget. None can be calibrated to an exact per-component target, which is what makes an apples-to-apples comparison awkward. Where the discussion below needs methods that meet the budget exactly, those are msPCA::mspca(), elasticnet::spca(), mixOmics::spca() and nsprcomp::nsprcomp().

Feasibility. Two things have to be separated here, because the answer depends on whether disjoint supports exist at all. On breast cancer and riboflavin, where pp is large relative to the total budget, orthogonality is nearly free: most methods return exactly orthogonal loadings simply because their supports do not overlap. On mtcars (p=11p = 11, 12 nonzeros) and Pitprops (p=13p = 13, 24 nonzeros) no disjoint solution exists, and that is where the differences appear.

There, msPCA::mspca() reaches 1e-4 while returning the requested cardinality exactly, and does so at every repetition: the largest violation it produced anywhere in the benchmark is 9.9e-05. Two other methods reach the tolerance on one dataset each, both with qualifications. nsprcomp::nscumcomp() reaches it on both, but only with gamma driven to 106–107, returning (5,5,2) and (5,6,5,2,4,2) against budgets of (4,4,4) and (4,4,4,4,4,4), and its worst Pitprops repetition is 1.03e-04. sklearn...SparsePCA() reaches it on mtcars by returning 11 nonzeros in total rather than the requested 12, which at p=11p = 11 admits a disjoint solution and so makes orthogonality free. Every other method, at the requested cardinality, returns violations between 0.08 and 0.56 on these two datasets.

The claim supported by this is narrower than “only msPCA can be feasible”, and more useful: it is the only method that delivers feasibility and the requested sparsity together, without a search over a penalty parameter to get there.

Variance explained. Among the methods that meet the requested cardinality, msPCA::mspca() and nsprcomp::nsprcomp() are generally the best performers, followed by mixOmics::spca() and elasticnet::spca(). msPCA does not appear to sacrifice variance explained in order to achieve feasibility.

Several methods post higher FVE while missing the budget, and those figures should be read in that light: sklearn...SparsePCA() reaches 0.907 on Pitprops at (7,3,4,3,5,4) with a violation of 0.815, and amanpg::spca.amanpg() 0.863 at a violation of 1.654. The exception is nscumcomp at 0.824 on mtcars with (5,5,2), which is both high and feasible, and is the most substantive competition in the comparison.

Reproducibility. Repeating each method under several seeds separates the deterministic implementations (elasticnet, PMA, sparsepca, mixOmics, amanpg, dense PCA) from the rest. nsprcomp and nscumcomp use random initialisation and move between runs; nsprcomp’s orthogonality violation on Pitprops spans 0.56–1.10. msPCA uses random restarts and is likewise not bit-reproducible across seeds, but its variation is confined to the objective. The feasibility guarantee holds at every seed on every dataset, the largest violation observed anywhere being 9.9e-05.

Memory. On the two high-dimensional datasets, where the memory column reflects the algorithms rather than fixed overheads, msPCA is the lightest of the sparse methods that respect an exact cardinality budget. On breast cancer it uses 3.1 MB on the data matrix against 79 MB for elasticnet on the same input and 209 MB in Gram mode, with sparsepca at 92 MB and nsprcomp and nscumcomp at 48–57 MB. On riboflavin it uses 45 MB against 309 MB for elasticnet. Within msPCA, the 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}-versus-𝑿\boldsymbol{X} choice matters more than the choice of package does between packages: the same function spans 641 MB to 45 MB on riboflavin depending on the interface.

Those figures are also more stable than the competitors’, for the reason given in the riboflavin section. For anyone sizing a job, a predictable memory requirement is worth as much as a small one, and the competing figures quoted here should be read as order-of-magnitude.

Scalability. msPCA::mspca() scales to datasets with pp in the thousands in reasonable time, and the type = "X" interface yields substantial runtime and memory gains when n≪pn \ll p: roughly 30x faster and 14x lighter on riboflavin. When n>pn > p, as in the Pitprops pseudo-data, the ordering reverses and type = "Sigma" is preferable.
